content: Lower respiratory tract infections are the leading cause of death from infectious diseases globally and rank as the fifth most common cause of death overall, according to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015. Vitamin C plays a role in modulating the body’s resistance to infectious agents, which suggests that supplementation with vitamin C could potentially help in preventing and treating pneumonia. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of vitamin C supplementation in preventing and treating pneumonia in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and two trial registries, up to March 4, 2020. References of relevant studies were also reviewed to identify additional research. No restrictions were applied regarding publication status or language. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs, which are studies that use non-random methods of allocation, such as date of birth or medical record numbers. These studies compared the effects of vitamin C supplementation with a control or placebo in preventing and treating pneumonia in children and adults. Five studies were included in the review, involving a total of 2,655 participants. Among these, two were RCTs, and three were quasi-RCTs. The studies were conducted in one high-income country (the USA) and three lower-middle-income countries (Bangladesh and Pakistan). Three studies were carried out in hospital inpatient settings, one in a school, and one in a military training center. The participants included children under five years of age in three studies, school-aged children in one study, and adults in one study. Two studies investigated the role of vitamin C supplementation in preventing pneumonia, while three studies examined its use as an adjunct to pneumonia treatment. For prevention, the studies used vitamin C doses of 1 gram daily for 14 weeks, 2 grams daily for 8 weeks, and 2 grams daily for 14 weeks. For treatment, the studies used doses of 125 mg daily and 200 mg daily, administered until symptoms resolved or the patient was discharged, in addition to standard pneumonia treatment. The overall quality of the included studies was judged to be at high or unclear risk of bias in terms of random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low. For the two studies assessing pneumonia prevention, the certainty of the evidence was very low, and the effect of vitamin C supplementation on pneumonia incidence and adverse events (such as urticaria) remains uncertain. None of these studies reported other primary outcomes, such as pneumonia prevalence or mortality, or any secondary outcomes. For the three studies evaluating vitamin C supplementation as an adjunct to pneumonia treatment, the certainty of the evidence was also very low. The effect of vitamin C supplementation on the duration of illness and hospitalization remains uncertain. None of these studies reported other primary or secondary outcomes. In conclusion, due to the small number of included studies and the very low certainty of the available evidence, the effect of vitamin C supplementation on the prevention and treatment of pneumonia remains uncertain. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the potential role of vitamin C in this context.
